name: Beth Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Beth, thanks for your time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say here is confidential. What's your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker for a private electricity company in the port city. Our crew does underground cables in the old town and the docks, plus the overhead lines out in the newer suburbs. It's my second year after the vocational certificate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We start at the Harbour Road depot, pick up the van, and usually spend the morning in a hole in the road with traffic going past, jointing cable or finding a fault the locator says is somewhere under a bus stop. My crew leader, Josie, is very calm and very precise, and I'm still slow with the jointing, she redoes maybe one in five of mine. I like that every street is a puzzle, there's a hundred years of old cables down there. What wears me out is the angry drivers, and the smell of the drains in August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that, back to work. I'm not one for big predictions either way. If someone at the depot was gloating, I'd probably just laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. Owen and I have a plan, I get my ticket, he grows his electrical business, and in a few years maybe I join him. Nothing changing means the plan stays on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep going with the apprenticeship and putting money into our joint savings, we're at about seven months' worth. Owen uses AI now and then to write his quotes, and I'd probably keep borrowing it to sum up the new cable standards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about Owen's business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a self-employed electrician, mostly houses, kitchens and new fuse boards. He started two years ago with one van and he's busy every week. We bought the flat above his workshop last year with both our savings, so between that and the money in the bank we're doing okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing at work you'd want to change, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The locator. It says the fault is here, we dig, and it's three metres over. If AI just made the locator better, I'd be happy and nobody would lose a job.

S0.say: Beth would say it's back to work and laugh off anyone gloating, since she doesn't go in for big predictions either way.
S0.think: Privately she'd be relieved, because the plan with her partner stays on track: she finishes her ticket, his electrical business grows, and she may join him.
S0.do: Carries on with her apprenticeship and keeps adding to joint savings of about seven months. Occasionally uses her partner's AI tool to summarise new cable standards.
S0.quote: If AI just made the locator better, I'd be happy and nobody would lose a job.
S0.fieldNote: Beth's life is tied closely to her partner's small business and their shared flat. She's practical and mild, without strong political framing. Her ideal AI is a better fault locator, which says a lot about how she sees technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work, and the sensible thing is to learn what's useful and ignore the rest. I'd say it at the depot, and probably to my parents, who worry about everything. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it nibbles at my job rather than eating it. The planning, the fault-finding, maybe the paperwork. But someone still has to go down the hole and join the cable, and the old town is a mess no robot is going to like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other crews pick up first. Once a tool had been used for a few months and Josie said it was any good, I'd learn it properly. I'd also help Owen set up AI for his bookings and quotes, because that might save him a day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but mostly it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this went badly for people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think it's one person's fault, it's more how things go. The company will try to save money, and the government will be slow. I'd want both to be sensible, which is probably asking a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our control room, the people who send us out and keep us safe while we're working. That's the kind of job software could take over. My friend Leila works there, she's the one who stays calm on the radio when things go wrong.

S1.say: Beth would tell colleagues and her worried parents that the sensible approach is to learn the useful tools and ignore the rest. She wouldn't post online.
S1.think: Privately she thinks AI nibbles at her job, taking planning, fault-finding and paperwork, but someone still has to join cable in the old town's tangled ground.
S1.do: Waits until other crews have used a tool for a few months and her crew leader approves, then learns it properly. Helps her partner set up AI for bookings and quotes to save him time.
S1.feel: A little uneasy but mostly feels it's manageable.
S1.quote: But someone still has to go down the hole and join the cable, and the old town is a mess no robot is going to like.
S1.fieldNote: Beth waits for proof from colleagues she trusts before adopting tools, a clear steady pattern. She blames no one and hopes for sensible behaviour from both company and government. Her concern for her friend in the control room was concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stay calm and work out what to do. People panicking at the depot wouldn't help anyone. I'd probably say it to my mum on the phone three times a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's both of us at once. My job and Owen's, because if robots can do hands-on work, they can wire a kitchen too. We'd still have the flat and some savings, but two years isn't long to work out a new life for two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd stop spending on anything big; Owen was going to buy a second van and that would wait. I'd keep working and save more, and we'd sit down every month and look at the numbers. If the work dried up, I'd look at what jobs were left around the port, maybe something checking or managing the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in the stomach, mostly when I think about Owen's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Owen's face?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his business is his baby. He'd built it from nothing. Mine's a job, his is his whole idea of himself, and watching that go would be worse than losing mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would two years change your plans as a couple, like where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold on to the flat, because it's paid off apart from a small loan. Moving wouldn't help, everywhere would be the same. If anything we'd stay put and spend less.

S2.say: Beth would urge calm at the depot, saying panic helps nobody, and repeat the same to her mother on the phone.
S2.think: Privately she sees it hitting both her job and her partner's business, since robots could wire kitchens too. They'd have the flat and savings, but two years is little time to rebuild two lives.
S2.do: Puts her partner's second van purchase on hold and saves more, reviewing the numbers with him monthly. Keeps working, then looks for remaining jobs around the port, such as checking or managing robots.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach when she thinks of her partner.
S2.quote: Mine's a job, his is his whole idea of himself, and watching that go would be worse than losing mine.
S2.fieldNote: Beth's anxiety in the fast picture is mainly about her partner's identity, not her own job. She responds with careful budgeting rather than drastic moves. Staying put in the flat is her anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast but doable if you start early. I'd tell the newer people at the depot to finish their tickets and learn the new kit as it comes. Same as always, I'm not one for speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years would let me finish my apprenticeship and get decent at jointing. I'd be qualified when it hits, which should count for something. And Owen would have time to shift his business toward something that lasts, like installing and maintaining the home robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish my modules and say yes to any training the company offered on new equipment, once I'd seen how it went for the first group. Owen and I would put away an extra 300 a month. We'd still buy the second van, but a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels like something we can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'once I'd seen how it went for the first group'. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first group always gets the buggy version. I've watched them roll out a new handheld at the depot and it crashed for a month. Let someone else find the bugs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, we're reacting. With five, we're choosing. That's really it.

S3.say: Beth would say five years is fast but doable with an early start, advising newer colleagues to finish their tickets and learn new kit as it arrives.
S3.think: Privately five years lets her qualify and get decent at jointing before it hits. She thinks her partner could shift toward installing and maintaining home robots.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship modules and takes company training on new equipment after the first group has tried it. Saves an extra 300 a month with her partner and buys a cheaper second van.
S3.quote: With two, we're reacting. With five, we're choosing.
S3.fieldNote: Five years changes Beth's posture from defence to choice, which she put in her own words. She still lets others go first with new tools. She and her partner plan as one unit, adjusting rather than cancelling purchases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for most people to sort themselves out. I'd say keep your head down, do your job well and learn as you go. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 37, fully qualified, with ten years of jointing behind me. I'd probably have joined Owen by then anyway. It still ends with the robots, so it's not nothing, but there's time to see how other people handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change very little the first year. Finish the ticket, keep saving, and start using AI more for study, because by then everyone at the depot would be. Over a few years, Owen and I would move the business toward whatever kept needing people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little worry at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said it'd still end with the robots. Does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. I'm not panicking, but I'd think about it on the drive home sometimes. Ten years goes fast. My parents always say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your parents to hear from you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're fine, and we have a plan. They came here with nothing, and Dad drove a taxi for thirty years. I'd want them to know their worrying paid off.

S4.say: Beth would say ten years gives most people enough time, advising colleagues to keep their heads down, do good work and learn as they go.
S4.think: Privately she'd be 37, qualified, with ten years of jointing, and probably in her partner's business already. It still ends with robots, but there's time to watch others adapt.
S4.do: Changes little in year one: finishes her ticket, keeps saving and uses AI more for study as colleagues do. Gradually moves the business with her partner toward work that still needs people.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little worry around the edges.
S4.quote: They came here with nothing, and Dad drove a taxi for thirty years. I'd want them to know their worrying paid off.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Beth relaxes into her existing plan and treats the ending as a background thought. Her parents' immigrant story sits behind her steady, careful habits. She'd learn more AI only once it became normal at the depot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Owen and I both get hit at the same time. What would help is some kind of income support for a year or two while people retrain, and the companies having to give proper notice, not just a letter on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about small businesses. Everyone talks about big companies and workers. Nobody talks about the guy with one van and a loan, and there are thousands of Owens.

headlineQuote: Nobody talks about the guy with one van and a loan, and there are thousands of Owens.
portrait: Beth Chen is a 27-year-old second-year lineworker on a city crew jointing underground cable in the old town and docks of a port city, still slow enough that her crew leader redoes some of her joints. She shares a flat above her partner Owen's workshop, and their joint plan hangs on his one-van electrical business. Practical and mild, she blames no one and adopts tools only after trusted colleagues have tested them. She's calm in the slow pictures, anxious when AGI comes in two years and hits both their livelihoods, and calm again with a decade to plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit her job and her partner's small business at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Income support for a year or two while people retrain, and rules making companies give proper notice.
